title: Why Cancer and Brain Tumours Are Increasingly Striking Younger Indians
excerpt: Indian doctors warn that ultra-processed foods, sedentary lifestyles, pollution, and late diagnosis are driving a surge in cancer cases among people under 40, with 20% of new diagnoses now in younger adults.
body:
• A Cancer Mukt Bharat Foundation study found 20% of cancer cases in India are now diagnosed in people under 40, with men making up 60% of young patients.
  • India reports over 28,000 brain tumour cases annually, with doctors noting a rising trend among younger adults previously considered low-risk.
  • Ultra-processed foods, sedentary lifestyles, environmental pollution, tobacco use, and obesity are identified as primary drivers of early-onset cancer.
  • Late diagnosis remains a critical problem — most patients reach specialists only after tumours have significantly advanced, when treatment is more complex and expensive.

Across hospitals in India, oncologists and neurologists are reporting a pattern that defies long-held assumptions: cancer and brain tumours are no longer diseases that mainly afflict the elderly. More patients in their 20s, 30s, and early 40s are walking into oncology wards with diagnoses that a generation ago would have been rare for their age group.

"We're seeing more brain tumour cases among younger people, which is extremely worrying," said Dr. Madhukar Bhardwaj, Director and HOD of Neurology at Aakash Healthcare, according to The Indian Practitioner. He listed seizures, personality changes, memory issues, vision problems, and loss of balance among the symptoms being reported — many of which patients initially dismiss as stress.

The Scale of the Problem

The numbers paint a stark picture. The International Association of Cancer Registries estimates that India reports over 28,000 brain tumour cases annually, with more than 24,000 deaths. The prevalence ranges from 5 to 10 per 100,000 population, though experts believe these figures are underestimated due to gaps in neuroimaging infrastructure and underreporting across rural India.

More broadly, a study by the Delhi-based Cancer Mukt Bharat Foundation found that 20% of all cancer cases in India are now diagnosed in people below 40. Men constitute 60% of these young patients, likely driven by higher rates of tobacco use, occupational exposure, and lifestyle factors, according to Madhyamam Online.

Up to 40% of colorectal cancer patients in India are now under 40 — a proportion far exceeding the 3-15% seen in Western countries, according to Dr. C. Bharath Kumar, Senior Consultant in Medical Gastroenterology at KIMS Hospitals Bengaluru.

What's Driving the Surge

"Ultra-processed foods and sedentary lifestyles are major contributors to the rising cancer rates among young Indians. The high intake of these foods, laden with unhealthy additives, combined with physical inactivity, is creating a health crisis."

— Dr. Rahul Bhargava, Director, Hematology and BMT, Fortis Memorial Research Institute

Doctors point to a convergence of factors. The shift toward ultra-processed diets, increased tobacco and alcohol consumption, sedentary work culture, rising obesity rates, and chronic stress all play a role. Environmental pollution in Indian cities — both air and water — exposes residents to carcinogenic substances from an early age.

A National Institutes of Health analysis covering 2010-2019 found that 14 cancer types have increased in incidence among people under 50 globally, including breast, colorectal, uterine, pancreatic, and testicular cancers. Some types, like thyroid and stomach cancers, rose only in younger age groups, according to OnlyMyHealth.

Dr. Satish Pawar, Senior Consultant in Surgical Oncology at CARE Hospitals in Hyderabad, noted that colorectal cancer — once rare in people under 40 — is now being reported in patients as young as 25. "Some of them have genetic risk factors, but many don't," he said.

The Diagnosis Gap

"Even now, patients often come to us after being treated for migraines or psychiatric conditions," said Dr. Aakaar Kapoor, CEO of City XRay and Scan Clinic, as reported by The Indian Practitioner. MRI and CT scans can detect tumours early, but most patients delay consulting a neurologist until symptoms become severe.

Dr. Ruchi Singh, HOD of Radiation Oncology at Asian Hospital, said that by the time many patients reach specialists, the tumour has progressed significantly. "Treatment becomes not only more complex but also more expensive, often involving surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy," she said.

Cost remains a barrier, particularly in low-income communities. While private hospitals have advanced facilities, many patients cannot afford treatment. Government hospitals see patients from smaller towns only at very late stages, according to Dr. Narendra Motarwar, Consultant in Neurosurgery at Jupiter Hospital.

What Experts Are Calling For

Medical professionals across India are pushing for expanded awareness campaigns targeting younger adults, improved diagnostic infrastructure in tier-2 cities and rural areas, and comprehensive support systems for patients and caregivers.

"India is witnessing a steady rise in brain tumour cases," said Dr. Praveen Gupta, Principal Director and Chief of Neurology. "We must act now — by raising awareness, investing in facilities in tier-2 and rural areas, and building strong support systems for patients and caregivers."

For diaspora Indians, the findings underscore the importance of early screening and not dismissing persistent symptoms — particularly in families with a history of cancer. The lifestyle factors driving the surge, from processed food consumption to sedentary habits, are equally prevalent in NRI communities worldwide.
nri_angle: Lifestyle factors driving early-onset cancer in India — processed foods, sedentary habits, pollution exposure — are equally prevalent in NRI communities, making early screening critical for diaspora Indians.
